name: Gelatin / bone broth

image.caption: Raspberry Gelatin Pineapple Sour Cream Salad

lead: Gelatin and bone broth are collagen-derived foods. Gelatin is made by partially breaking down animal collagen, mostly from pork skin, bones and cattle hides, and bone broth is a long-simmered stock in which collagen converts to gelatin. Wellness and looksmaxxing communities eat them to support skin, hair and joints.

Proponents reason that eating collagen-derived amino acids supplies building blocks for skin and hair. Regulators and reference sources report that a cause-and-effect link between ingested collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance has not been established, and no studies of appearance outcomes were found.

paras: People drink bone broth as a daily or regular warm drink or cooking base, or eat gelatin as dessert or stirred into drinks. It is used as part of an overall diet alongside other protein. Users who report skin or hair changes describe weeks to months.

Gelatin is a protein food and is generally treated as low risk, though some people are allergic to gelatin in injected drugs. It is not suitable for vegetarian, halal or kosher practice depending on the source.

chain: Building blocks for skin and hair
angle.text: Fans eat gelatin and bone broth because collagen-derived amino acids are thought to supply building blocks for skin and hair. Reference sources report that a link between ingested collagen and joint maintenance has not been established, and no appearance studies were found.

lead: Gelatin and bone broth are collagen-derived foods. Gelatin is made by partially breaking down animal collagen, mostly from pork skin, bones and cattle hides, and gels in water [1]. Bone broth is a long-simmered stock of animal bones and connective tissue, in which collagen converts to gelatin and thickens the liquid [2].

In looksmaxxing and wellness circles they are discussed as dietary "collagen foods" that proponents associate with skin, hair and joint appearance. Regulators and reference sources report that a cause-and-effect link between ingested collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance has not been established, and one encyclopedia summary states there is no scientific evidence supporting many of the health claims made for bone broth [2][1][3].
infobox: Animal collagen, converted to gelatin by simmering
About 98 to 99% protein, not a complete protein [1]
Bone broth popularised by the early 2010s [2]

paras: Stock made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables is a traditional cooking base; the connective tissue releases collagen that becomes gelatin and gives the liquid body [2]. Gelatin itself is used in desserts, confectionery, capsules and cosmetics, and can be made at home by boiling cartilage-rich bones or cuts [1].
Dry gelatin is nearly all protein, but it lacks tryptophan and is low in several other amino acids; glycine, proline and hydroxyproline make up roughly half of its amino acids [1].

Gelatin-like dishes appear in a 10th-century Arabic cookbook and a 14th-century French recipe, and extraction methods improved in the 1700s and 1800s [1]. The bone broth health trend took off by the early 2010s, with the 2014 book Nourishing Broth credited with promoting claims about its nutrient density [2].

Proponents link collagen foods to skin, hair and joint health. The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that a cause-and-effect relationship between collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance had not been established [1][3]. Reference summaries note that hydrolysed collagen is used in creams as a conditioner and moisturiser, which concerns topical use rather than eating [1][3]. Regulators consider the disease-transmission risk from bovine bone gelatin very low under standard processing, and some people are allergic to gelatin in injected drugs [1].
No studies found. Related research on hydrolysed collagen as a wound dressing has been reported, but it concerns topical medical use and not dietary gelatin or broth for appearance [1][3].
